name: LLM / AI-gateway feature backend (token velocity, jailbreak velocity, agent quotas)
parent_research_topic: Beava use cases — current and potential applications of beava as a real-time feature server

domain_fit.domain_name: LLM / AI-gateway feature backend — per-API-key, per-tenant, per-agent real-time usage, abuse and cost features for AI gateways, agent platforms and MCP servers
domain_fit.one_line_definition: An AI gateway (Portkey / LiteLLM / Helicone / Bifrost / Truefoundry / Envoy AI Gateway / Kong AI Gateway / Cloudflare AI Gateway / agentgateway) or MCP gateway decides in <10 ms on every model call whether to allow, throttle, downgrade, fall-back, redact, challenge or hard-stop based on rolling per-(API-key, tenant, agent, model, route, user) tokens-per-minute (TPM), requests-per-minute (RPM), tool-call frequency, jailbreak-attempt velocity, cost-spend velocity and agent-step counters computed live from the request/response stream.
domain_fit.representative_jobs_to_be_done: 1) Enforce token-aware budgets — tokens-per-minute (TPM), tokens-per-hour, tokens-per-day, $-per-team — per-API-key, per-virtual-key, per-tenant, per-team, per-model (the LiteLLM / Portkey / Truefoundry / Bifrost / agentgateway core feature). 2) Detect runaway autonomous agents — bound steps-per-session, tool-calls-per-minute, recursive-self-call ratios, identical-tool-call repetitions before a Claude / OpenAI / Gemini loop burns $437 / $3,000 / $47,000 (real public incidents). 3) Rate-limit jailbreak / prompt-injection velocity — per-API-key count of guardrail-flagged prompts in 1m/5m/1h, count of high-similarity-to-known-jailbreak-corpus prompts, ratio of refused-to-accepted completions — to ban or quarantine abusive keys before a successful bypass. 4) Per-tenant cost meter — $-spent-per-minute / hour / day per tenant, customer, feature, user_id, broken out by model and prompt-type — feeds the dashboard the FinOps / billing team actually pays for. 5) Adaptive throttling on provider 429 / 5xx signals — when (api_key, model) sees rolling rate of upstream 429 spike, automatically tighten the local budget for that key/model pair so retries don't worsen the storm. 6) Feed an ML / classifier scorer with per-entity behavioral features for high-risk-traffic classification (legitimate agentic load vs scripted abuse vs jailbreak-fuzzing).
domain_fit.event_shapes: Wire events emitted by the gateway / proxy / MCP server on every call. Primary events: llm_request {ts, api_key_hash, virtual_key_id, tenant_id, team_id, user_id_hash, agent_id, session_id, trace_id, model, provider, route, prompt_tokens, max_tokens, prompt_hash, prompt_embedding (optional), tool_called (if any), is_streaming, status_code, latency_ms}; llm_response {ts, request_id, completion_tokens, total_tokens, finish_reason, refused (bool), guardrail_flags[], cost_usd, ttft_ms}; guardrail_hit {ts, api_key_hash, tenant_id, prompt_id, rule_id (jailbreak / pii / toxicity / off-topic), severity, classifier_score, action (allow / flag / redact / block)}; tool_call {ts, agent_id, session_id, tool_name, args_hash, duration_ms, error}; agent_step {ts, agent_id, session_id, step_index, parent_step}; provider_throttle {ts, model, provider, http_status (429/529/503), retry_after_ms}. Volume is dominated by llm_request / llm_response (one of each per call) and tool_call (multiple per agent step).
domain_fit.feature_shapes: Heavy use of counters, sums (for tokens / cost), rates, n_unique, distributions and entropy over 1s / 10s / 1m / 5m / 1h / 24h sliding windows. Per-api_key: sum(prompt_tokens) and sum(completion_tokens) over 1m / 1h / 24h (TPM / TPH / TPD), rate(requests) (RPM), sum(cost_usd), rate(refused), rate(guardrail_hit), distribution(model), distribution(finish_reason), n_unique(session_id). Per-(api_key x model): TPM, $-per-minute, p99(prompt_tokens) — needed because Anthropic / OpenAI enforce TPM per-model. Per-tenant / per-team: same set, aggregated. Per-(api_key x rule_id): rate(guardrail_hit) — jailbreak-velocity per key per attack family. Per-agent_id: count(tool_call) over 10s / 1m, n_unique(tool_name), entropy(tool_name distribution) (low entropy = stuck in a loop), count(identical args_hash in 1m) (repeat-tool-call detector), max(step_index), recursive_self_call_ratio. Per-session_id: same agent features bounded to the session. Per-model: rate(provider 429) for upstream-pressure-aware throttling. Per-tenant cost meter: rolling sum(cost_usd) with TTL aligned to billing period. Distance features: distance(prompt_embedding, known_jailbreak_centroid) for similarity-to-jailbreak detection (requires embedding-aware distance primitive or pre-computed similarity score on the producer side).
domain_fit.entity_grain: Composite and dense. Primary keys are api_key_hash, virtual_key_id (LiteLLM concept), tenant_id, team_id, user_id_hash, agent_id, session_id, trace_id, model, route. Cross products that matter: (api_key x model) (provider-side TPM is per-model), (tenant x model), (agent_id x tool_name), (api_key x rule_id) (jailbreak family velocity), (tenant x user_id) (per-end-user attribution inside a SaaS), (session_id x step_index). Notably tenant_id and api_key_hash are bounded / slowly-growing (vendor SaaS customer count), while session_id and trace_id are explosive (sub-second TTL).
domain_fit.window_semantics_required: Sliding windows dominate for abuse / velocity (1s, 10s, 1m, 5m, 1h, 24h). Tumbling windows are required for billing-grade per-tenant cost meters and per-key TPM accounting that must align to provider billing periods (1m / 1h / 24h calendar tumbling). Session windows are required for per-session agent-step / tool-call counters that should reset on session end. Provider-side TPM / RPM is typically per-rolling-minute, so a 1m sliding sum is the canonical feature. Approximate aggregates (HLL for n_unique sessions per tenant, CMS / Top-K for top tool names per agent) are acceptable on the explosive (session, trace) axes; exact integer sums are required on token / cost counters that feed billing.
domain_fit.exactly_once_or_idempotency_needs: Mixed and important. Abuse-velocity features tolerate at-least-once (double-count biases velocity upward, which is the safe direction). Billing-grade per-tenant $-spend meters and provider-TPM enforcement counters require strict no-double-count — typically achieved via request_id idempotency at the producer (LiteLLM virtual-key spend, agentgateway response-time token check). Buyers most often run a separate exact billing counter (with idempotency-key dedupe and durable log) and use the streaming feature backend only for the abuse / safety / adaptive-throttle signal — but a feature backend that ships exactly-once via dedup-on-request_id would compress that stack into one component.

technical_fit.latency_budget: Read p99 <5 ms is the operational target for the inline decision; <10 ms is the hard ceiling because every model call is gated. Best-in-class numbers in this market: Bifrost ~11 microseconds mean overhead at 5k RPS, Helicone <5 ms p95 in Rust, Truefoundry <5 ms p95, Envoy AI Gateway 1–3 ms overhead, Kong AI Gateway 2–5 ms, Cloudflare AI Gateway 10–50 ms (proxy hop), LiteLLM degrades sharply above ~500 RPS due to Python GIL. Beava's sub-ms TCP+msgpack get / batch_get sits cleanly inside the budget when co-located on the same host or pod as the gateway; an off-host hop already eats most of the budget against the microsecond-class competitors.
technical_fit.feature_freshness_sla: Sub-second to single-digit seconds. A 1m TPM enforcement decision cannot tolerate a feature that lags by 10 s — provider-side enforcement is on a rolling 60 s window, and any local approximation that is older than the upstream window risks either over-rejecting (false positive) or letting the key blow through the provider limit (false negative, the worse outcome). Agent runaway-loop detection on a 10 s window needs sub-second freshness; the public $437 / $3,000 / $47,000 runaway incidents accumulated cost within minutes. Beava's push-on-event model with no broker hop fits this — comparable AI-gateway products use Redis or in-process counters precisely because Kafka/Kinesis hop is too slow.
technical_fit.throughput_profile: Steady-state is write-heavy: each model call is 1–2 events (request + response) plus 0–N tool-call events; each gateway decision triggers 1 batch_get of 10–50 features. A mid-size AI-platform tenant runs 1–100 RPS sustained (Portkey runs ~400B+ tokens / day across 200+ enterprises = ~5M tokens/sec aggregate, but per-tenant); a large enterprise AI gateway runs 1–5k RPS aggregate; a hyperscale AI gateway (OpenAI internal, Cloudflare AI Gateway) is far beyond. Bifrost has been stress-tested at 5,000 RPS sustained with 11 microsecond overhead and Maxim claims 50x LiteLLM. Beava's published ~684k EPS (M4, TCP+msgpack, parallel=16) is two orders of magnitude above the per-tenant rate at a typical AI-gateway buyer, and roughly matches an entire vendor's aggregate inline-decision rate; one beava node likely covers a single-region AI-gateway tenant comfortably. [uncertain]
technical_fit.read_to_write_ratio: Roughly 1:1 with a read-skew when streaming. Each call produces 1 request event + 1 response event = 2 writes, plus 0–N tool-call writes, and 1 batch_get of many features on the decision path. Streaming completions produce 1 write per token / chunk if instrumented at that grain, which pushes the profile write-heavy in long-context / agentic workloads. Distinctly less read-heavy than recsys ranking, distinctly less write-heavy than ad-tech telemetry; closest analog is the API-abuse / WAF profile (#15b).
technical_fit.state_size_estimate: Dominated by tenant / api_key / agent / session cardinality. A mid-size AI-platform vendor sees 1k–100k active virtual keys, 100–10k tenants, 10k–10M concurrent agent sessions/day, 100k–10M unique users/day. At ~300 B per per-entity feature vector (TPM, RPM, $-spend, refused-rate, model-mix histogram, tool-mix histogram, agent-step counters), keys+tenants+teams fit in single-digit GB easily; session/trace state at 10M/day with multi-hour TTL is 1–10 GB and lives well in beava's in-memory model. A hyperscale buyer (Cloudflare AI Gateway, OpenAI gateway-side enforcement) would need horizontal sharding by tenant_id, which beava v0 lacks. [uncertain]
technical_fit.cardinality_pattern: Bounded on model / provider / route / rule_id (low hundreds globally). Slowly-growing on tenant_id, team_id, api_key_hash (thousands to low millions across a SaaS-platform's customers). Slowly-growing on agent_id (per-tenant agent definitions, bounded). Explosive on session_id, trace_id, user_id_hash, prompt_hash (sub-second to hour-class TTL is required). The (agent_id x tool_name) cross-product is bounded (low thousands per agent); (api_key x model) is bounded (key x ~50 models); (tenant x user_id) is the explosive axis for large SaaS deployments.
technical_fit.typical_state_lifecycle_and_ttl: Tiered: seconds for 1s/10s sliding counters; 1m for provider-TPM enforcement; 1h–24h for hot reputation and rolling cost; 7–30d for medium-term abuse reputation feeding ML; 30–90d retention is typically exported to an OLAP/lakehouse (BigQuery, Snowflake, ClickHouse) for FinOps reporting and EU AI Act Article 12 logging (6-month minimum retention for high-risk systems, takes effect Aug 2, 2026). Aggressive per-session TTL is essential because trace/session cardinality is explosive.
technical_fit.typical_feature_count_per_decision: 20–60 features per inline gateway decision. Typical batch_get on an AI-gateway hot path: per-key TPM, RPM, $-spent-min/hour, refused-rate, guardrail-hit-rate per rule_id (~5 rule families), per-(key x model) TPM, per-tenant TPM and $-spend, per-agent_id step count, tool-call rate, identical-tool-call count, recursive-call ratio, provider-side 429 rate for the target model. Beava's batch_get path is a natural fit.
technical_fit.durability_requirements: Best-effort to crash-safe for abuse / adaptive-throttle features; regulator-grade where the same counter is repurposed for $-spend / billing or EU AI Act Article 12 logging. The pragmatic split: hot feature counters live in beava (WAL + snapshot is fine, a few minutes of feature loss on restart is acceptable for adaptive limits), while the durable audit log goes to a separate append-only store (lakehouse / Loki / Splunk) so the regulator-grade obligation does not live in an in-memory feature backend. EU AI Act Article 12 requires 6 months of automatic event logs for high-risk systems — beava is the wrong store for that retention, but is the right store for the live derived features computed from those events.
technical_fit.deployment_topology_fit: Excellent fit for sidecar / per-cluster / per-pod topology that AI-gateway vendors use. Helicone ships as a 15MB single Rust binary with sub-5ms p95; Bifrost is a Go binary with 11 microsecond overhead; agentgateway, Envoy AI Gateway and Kong AI Gateway are all proxy-binary topologies. Beava's single-binary, no-broker, in-memory model maps directly to a sidecar next to the gateway. Hard limits: (a) no TLS / no auth on :8080/:8081/:8090 in v0 disqualifies any deployment that needs mTLS between the gateway and the feature backend (almost every regulated buyer); (b) no in-process sharding limits a single tenant to one box; (c) no cross-node feature replication / merge — agentgateway already distinguishes 'local' vs 'global' (Redis-backed) rate-limiting precisely because cluster-wide quota coordination matters; (d) refuse-on-network-FS is acceptable per-pod but constrains the durability story.

commercial_fit.who_buys: ML-platform / AI-platform-engineering / SRE / FinOps / AI-safety / SecOps teams at: (a) standalone AI-gateway vendors (Portkey, LiteLLM/BerriAI, Helicone, Bifrost/Maxim, Truefoundry, agentgateway/Solo.io, requesty), (b) general-purpose API/proxy vendors with AI gateway products (Kong AI Gateway, Envoy AI Gateway / Tetrate, Cloudflare AI Gateway, Apigee, Tyk, KrakenD, Zuplo, Traefik Hub), (c) MCP-gateway vendors (MintMCP, agentgateway, Composio, Lasso), (d) agent platforms and observability vendors that need quota / abuse signals (LangSmith, AgentOps, Langfuse, Galileo, Arize, Langwatch, Helicone observability, Datadog LLM Observability), (e) LLM-safety / guardrail vendors that need velocity context for their classifiers (Lakera, Protect AI, Prompt Security, NeMo Guardrails users, HiddenLayer, Robust Intelligence), (f) in-house ML-platform teams at large enterprises building an internal AI gateway (Citi, Bank of America, JPMC, Goldman, large healthcare and retail enterprises). Distinctly NOT the application-developer using Anthropic / OpenAI directly without a gateway — buyer here is platform-eng or infra.
commercial_fit.market_size_signal: LLM Middleware Gateway market: ~$18.9M in 2026 projected to ~$189M by 2034 (~49.6% CAGR per Intel Market Research). Enterprise LLM market: ~$5.91B in 2026 projected to ~$48.25B by 2034 (~30% CAGR per Fortune Business Insights). Public scale signals: Portkey processes 2.5+ trillion tokens across 650+ organizations; LiteLLM is the most-starred open-source LLM proxy (~46.8k GitHub stars); Helicone (~5.2k stars, YC W23); Portkey Gateway (~10.9k stars); Bifrost (~4.9k stars). Vendor pricing: Portkey enterprise tier, Truefoundry / Helicone / Bifrost are enterprise contracts, Cloudflare AI Gateway is bundled into Workers. Real cost-pressure signals: documented runaway-agent incidents at $437 (single overnight session), $3,000 (single Claude Opus loop), $47,000 (LangChain retry loop over 11 days, or 127k API calls in 8 hours) — direct demand drivers for the agent-quota use case. Provider-side scale: OpenAI Tier 5 is 40M TPM; Anthropic Claude Tier 4 is 4M ITPM for Haiku, 2M for Sonnet — enterprise customers run their own gateway-side enforcement of these limits. [uncertain]
commercial_fit.urgency_drivers: 1) Documented runaway-agent cost incidents in 2025–2026 ($47k LangChain loop, $437 overnight, $3k per Claude Opus loop) — every AI-platform buyer now wants hard token / step / cost ceilings. 2) Anthropic and OpenAI rate-limit tightening / sub-tier shuffles forced gateway-side TPM / RPM enforcement (LiteLLM, Portkey, Truefoundry, Bifrost, agentgateway all shipped this in 2025–2026). 3) MCP / agentic-AI explosion in 2025–2026 — autonomous agents make 1,000+ tool calls / min and 'Agentic DoS' is now a named category; MCP gateways (MintMCP, Composio, agentgateway, Lasso) ship rate-limiting as core feature. 4) EU AI Act Article 12 logging requirements for high-risk AI systems take effect Aug 2, 2026 (6-month minimum retention; up to EUR 15M / 3% global turnover penalties) — pulls logging + monitoring + quota controls into compliance budget. 5) OWASP LLM Top 10 LLM01 (Prompt Injection) and LLM04 (Model DoS) frame the jailbreak-velocity and resource-consumption controls; LLM10 (unbounded consumption) is explicit. 6) AI-gateway / LLM-gateway market is exploding (49.6% CAGR) and every vendor is racing to ship per-key / per-tenant / per-agent quota + abuse features — first-mover advantage on a real-time feature backend is open. 7) FinOps for AI is the 2026 dashboard — per-tenant / per-user cost attribution is now a board-level number at any SaaS shipping LLM features.
commercial_fit.regulatory_or_audit_constraints: EU AI Act (Reg. 2024/1689): Article 12 (Record-keeping for high-risk AI), Article 26 (Deployer obligations) — automatic logging of events relevant for risk identification and post-market monitoring; minimum 6 months retention; high-risk obligations effective Aug 2, 2026; penalties up to EUR 15M or 3% global turnover. OWASP LLM Top 10 2025 (LLM01 Prompt Injection, LLM04 Model Denial of Service, LLM10 Unbounded Consumption) is the de-facto controls framework. NIST AI RMF (US) for federal / regulated buyers. GDPR / CCPA for prompt and completion content (PII, salted user_id_hash, short TTLs). SOC 2 and ISO 27001 for any AI-SaaS vendor. PCI-DSS / HIPAA where prompts contain protected data (healthcare AI gateways). Industry-specific: FFIEC / OCC AI guidance for US financial buyers; DORA (in force Jan 17, 2025) for EU FS firms includes ICT third-party / AI exposure controls.
commercial_fit.time_to_value_signal: Very fast — 1–3 days to a runnable demo of per-(api_key, model) TPM + RPM + $-spend + jailbreak-hit-rate + tool-call velocity with @bv.event + @bv.table primitives plus a thin LiteLLM / Portkey / Helicone / agentgateway plugin (or an Envoy Wasm filter, or a Kong / Tyk Lua plugin) that pushes the request/response events and pulls batch_get. 2–6 weeks to a production pilot at an AI-gateway vendor once TLS, auth and a Rust / Go client SDK are added. A demo video showing 'shut down a runaway $47k LangChain loop in 8 seconds' or 'detect jailbreak-velocity ramp before key spends $1000' should be straightforward and lead-generation-grade.

competition.incumbents: Generic real-time stack: Redis (counters + Lua) is the overwhelming default — LiteLLM, Portkey, Truefoundry, agentgateway, Kong, Tyk, Apigee all use Redis (or sometimes DragonflyDB / Memcached) for distributed TPM / RPM / virtual-key budget. agentgateway exposes a 'local' (in-process) vs 'global' (Redis-backed) rate-limit choice and explicitly documents the latency / consistency trade-off. Cloudflare Durable Objects for serverless-edge AI-gateway quota. In-process Go / Rust counters for single-replica deploys (Bifrost, Helicone). Flink / Materialize / RisingWave only show up at large enterprises that already have Kafka pipelines feeding their AI-platform analytics. Online feature stores (Tecton, Hopsworks, Chalk, Fennel, Feast) are positioned for ML-model serving, not inline gateway decisions; Chalk and Fennel could pivot here but have not shipped LLM-specific gateway integrations. [uncertain]
competition.competitive_incumbent_per_domain: Standalone AI gateways (each ships built-in rate-limit / budget / abuse features): Portkey (2.5T tokens, 650+ orgs, 10.9k stars), LiteLLM (46.8k stars, Redis-backed virtual keys), Helicone (Rust, ~5.2k stars, 15MB binary, <5ms p95, YC W23), Bifrost / Maxim AI (~4.9k stars, Go, 11 microsecond overhead at 5k RPS), Truefoundry (enterprise budget controls + RBAC), Requesty (EU-compliant routing), agentgateway / Solo.io (v1.0 in 2026, MCP/A2A native, local+global rate limit), TensorZero. Hyperscaler / proxy AI gateways: Cloudflare AI Gateway (free tier, 10–50ms overhead, SaaS-only), Envoy AI Gateway (Tetrate, 1–3ms overhead), Kong AI Gateway (2–5ms, OPA integration, advanced features behind enterprise), Apigee, Tyk, KrakenD, Zuplo. MCP gateways: MintMCP, Composio, agentgateway, Lasso, Splunk MCP Server beta. Agent-observability with cost / step tracking: LangSmith, AgentOps, Galileo, Arize, Langfuse, Langwatch, Datadog LLM Observability, OpenLLMetry / Traceloop, Helicone observability, MLflow AI monitoring. Guardrail / safety vendors that benefit from velocity context: Lakera, Protect AI, Prompt Security, HiddenLayer, Robust Intelligence, NeMo Guardrails, Snowflake Cortex Guardrails.
competition.beava_differentiator: 1) Single binary, no Kafka / Flink / Redis cluster — matches the topology this market is converging on (one Helicone / Bifrost / agentgateway binary per cluster or per pod). 2) 50+ aggregation primitives (counters, n_unique, velocity, rate, distribution, distance, entropy) cover the per-(api_key x model), per-tenant, per-agent feature set this domain literally lives on; competitors hand-roll these in Redis + Lua. 3) Sub-ms TCP+msgpack get / batch_get is inside the <5ms inline-decision budget that AI-gateway buyers are measured on (Helicone <5ms, Truefoundry <5ms, Envoy 1–3ms, Bifrost 11 microseconds). 4) Apache-2.0 with no open-core — attractive to AI-gateway vendors (LiteLLM is MIT, Helicone Apache-2.0, Bifrost Apache-2.0, agentgateway Apache-2.0) that want to embed it rather than depend on Redis Source-Available or a competitor's managed cloud. 5) Push-on-event model maps directly to how gateways already emit per-call request/response events — no Kafka hop between gateway and feature backend. 6) Composite keys ((api_key x model), (tenant x user), (agent_id x tool_name)) are first-class via @bv.table rather than a Redis key-naming convention. 7) Per-entity feature vectors with 20–60 features each fit beava's batch_get exactly — competitors use 10+ Redis round-trips per decision or unsafe Lua mega-scripts. 8) The 'velocity' concept (rolling-rate of guardrail-flag, refused-completion, identical-tool-call) is a natural beava primitive but a tedious Redis script — material developer-experience win for safety teams. 9) Beava's @bv.event Python decorator model fits the ML-platform persona (the buyer here, unlike the WAF buyer at #15b who is in Rust / Lua / Wasm).
competition.where_beava_loses_today: 1) No TLS / no auth on :8080 / :8081 / :8090 in v0 — disqualifying for any deployment where the AI gateway and feature backend are not in the same trust domain (i.e., almost every production deployment). This is the single biggest blocker; Portkey, LiteLLM, Helicone, Bifrost, Truefoundry, agentgateway all ship with mTLS / API-key / OAuth on day one. 2) No in-process sharding — a hyperscale AI-gateway vendor running multi-million-tenant SaaS cannot horizontally scale within one beava cluster. 3) No cross-node feature replication / merge / CRDT counters — competing AI gateways use Redis precisely so their TPM / RPM counters are cluster-consistent across N gateway replicas (agentgateway explicitly distinguishes 'local' vs 'global' rate-limit and documents the consistency trade-off). 4) In-memory only with refuse-on-network-FS — large per-tenant cost meters that need calendar-month retention must export to an external store; beava is the wrong place for the audit retention obligation under EU AI Act Article 12 (6 months). 5) No triggers / 'fire when counter crosses threshold' — adaptive throttling and runaway-agent kill-switch genuinely want event-driven hooks ('when (agent_id).identical_tool_calls_60s > 50, fire webhook to kill session'), and polling-with-batch_get is wasteful on the hot path. 6) No multi-tenancy primitives (per-tenant namespaces, quotas, isolation) — every AI-gateway vendor serving many customers needs these on day one. 7) No first-class embedding-distance or vector primitive — jailbreak-similarity detection (distance(prompt_embedding, known_jailbreak_centroid)) is best done with cosine-similarity in a vector index; beava can store the precomputed score, but if the buyer wants the embedding compare to happen in the feature backend they will look elsewhere. [uncertain] 8) No SDK in Rust / Go / TypeScript / Java — the AI-gateway buyer ecosystem is in Go (Bifrost, agentgateway), Rust (Helicone), TypeScript (Portkey, many MCP gateways) and Python (LiteLLM). Python SDK is great for LiteLLM and for ML-platform teams; the wire is language-agnostic but the SDK matrix is the gap. 9) No 'top-k tenants by $-spend last 5 min' analyst query surface — FinOps dashboards want this and today need a separate export. 10) No content-aware features (only structured-event aggregation) — buyers wanting to score 'jailbreak similarity' from the prompt text in-process need to bolt on a separate classifier; this may be a feature, not a bug.
competition.integration_surface: Producers (AI gateways emitting per-call events): LiteLLM (Python proxy, OpenAI-format, virtual keys, custom callbacks); Portkey Gateway (TypeScript / Node, plugin / hook architecture); Helicone (Rust, Tower middleware); Bifrost / Maxim (Go, plugin SDK); Truefoundry (Node.js backend); agentgateway (Rust, MCP/A2A); Kong AI Gateway (OpenResty + Lua plugins); Envoy AI Gateway (Wasm / ext_proc filters); Apigee, Tyk, Zuplo, KrakenD, Cloudflare AI Gateway (Workers). MCP-specific producers: MintMCP, Composio, agentgateway, Lasso, Splunk MCP. Agent SDKs that could push directly: LangChain / LangGraph callbacks, OpenAI Agents SDK, Anthropic Computer Use SDK, AutoGen, CrewAI, Pydantic AI. Observability producers via OpenTelemetry: OpenLLMetry / Traceloop, Datadog LLM Observability, Sentry AI, MLflow AI Monitoring (any of these can fan out to beava as a second sink). Consumers: gateway policy layers (OPA, Kong plugins, Envoy filters), kill-switches (webhook -> session cancel), FinOps dashboards (Grafana, custom UIs), classifier scorers (XGBoost / DeBERTa / small LLM-as-judge consuming velocity features as side-channel).
competition.scoring_engine_coupling: Both — but lean toward rules engine. The dominant pattern in this market is a deterministic rules layer (per-key TPM < X; per-agent identical_tool_calls_60s < Y; per-tenant $-spend / hour < $Z) combined with an optional ML classifier for jailbreak / abuse scoring. Beava as a pure feature backend stays decoupled — the gateway implements the rule with batch_get + comparison, and the classifier reads the same features as side input. Concretely: LiteLLM / Portkey / Truefoundry / agentgateway are rules-first; Lakera / Prompt Security / NeMo Guardrails are classifier-first; Helicone has both layers. beava feeds all of them identically.

adoption_signals.adversarial_pressure_level: High and rising. Jailbreak / prompt-injection is an actively adversarial domain — attackers retool weekly (FlipAttack, PAIR, character-injection bypass, encoded-prompt families, agentic-fuzzing), and recent empirical work shows up to 100% evasion rates against Azure Prompt Shield and Meta Prompt Guard. Cost-abuse / agent-runaway pressure is less adversarial but high-impact (a single misbehaving customer agent loop costs the vendor four to five figures per overnight). Provider-side rate-limit evasion (key rotation, account farming) is moderately adversarial. The feature-drift expectation is high: the buyer wants to add and retire features continuously (new jailbreak family lands on Friday, gateway must detect by Monday), which argues for a developer-ergonomic feature backend (beava's @bv.event / @bv.table model) over a SQL-on-Flink pipeline.

risk_and_non_goals.non_goals: 1) Storing the full prompt / completion text — beava is in-memory only; prompts and completions belong in a durable log (Loki / Splunk / S3 / lakehouse) for EU AI Act Article 12 (6-month retention) and forensic replay. 2) Computing embeddings or running classifier models in-process — distance-to-jailbreak-centroid requires a vector store / similarity index (FAISS, pgvector, Qdrant, Pinecone) or a classifier (DeBERTa, Lakera, Prompt Guard); beava stores the precomputed score, not the embedding pipeline. 3) Acting as the AI gateway itself — beava sits behind one (LiteLLM, Portkey, Helicone, Bifrost, Truefoundry, agentgateway, Kong AI, Envoy AI), feeding it features. 4) Acting as the policy engine or kill-switch — beava is the feature backend, not the decision point. 5) Long historical cost / FinOps reporting (calendar-month, calendar-quarter) — beava is wrong for retention; that belongs in a warehouse. 6) Strict exactly-once billing-grade $-spend counters where double-counting is unacceptable — buyers should keep a separate exact counter (idempotency-key dedupe + durable log) for invoicing; beava covers the abuse / adaptive-throttle / observability signal. 7) Audit-grade record-keeping for EU AI Act Article 12 / NIST AI RMF — different store, different SLO. 8) Cross-tenant joins / 'show me all api_keys with similar prompt patterns' — beava has no join engine; that is an OLAP / vector-DB problem. 9) Replacing observability platforms (LangSmith, AgentOps, Galileo, Arize) — beava is the velocity feature backend they would build on, not a replacement for tracing / span storage / replay.
risk_and_non_goals.open_engineering_gaps: Concrete features beava would need to ship to be production-grade for this domain, roughly in priority order: 1) TLS termination + mTLS on :8081 / :8090, plus an auth model (token / mTLS / OAuth) on the admin and push surfaces — without this, no AI-gateway / MCP-gateway vendor can deploy externally and no enterprise buyer with an internal AI gateway can deploy at all. The single biggest blocker; every competing AI gateway ships mTLS / OAuth / JWT on day one. 2) Multi-tenancy primitives: per-tenant namespaces, per-tenant quotas, per-tenant rate limits on the admin surface, per-tenant isolation — AI-gateway vendors serving many customers need this on day one. 3) Triggers / 'callback when counter crosses threshold' — runaway-agent kill-switches and adaptive provider-aware throttling want event-driven hooks (e.g., 'when (agent_id).identical_tool_calls_60s > 50, fire webhook to kill session'); polling with batch_get adds avoidable round-trips on the inline hot path. 4) Cross-node feature replication / merge (CRDT counters, gossip, anti-entropy, or Redis-style global mode) — agentgateway explicitly distinguishes 'local' (per-replica) vs 'global' (Redis-backed) rate-limit; a multi-replica gateway deployment needs the global option, or buyers default to Redis. 5) Rust / Go / TypeScript / Java client SDKs — the AI-gateway buyer ecosystem is in Go (Bifrost, agentgateway), Rust (Helicone), TypeScript (Portkey, MCP gateways) and Python (LiteLLM). Wire is language-agnostic; SDK matrix is the gap. 6) First-class HLL / CMS / Top-K approximate primitives prominently documented, for explosive session / trace / user cardinality and 'top-k tenants by $-spend' analyst queries. 7) Tumbling-window primitives aligned to calendar boundaries (per-minute / per-hour / per-day) for provider-TPM enforcement — provider rate limits are typically rolling-60-second, so a 1m sliding sum is needed too, but billing-grade per-tenant cost meters want calendar-aligned tumbling. 8) Idempotency-on-request_id (exactly-once writes) so the same counter can be reused for billing-adjacent accounting. 9) Bounded cold-start WAL replay benchmarks with multi-GB hot state — a node restart during an active jailbreak / runaway-agent storm cannot become an outage. 10) GDPR-friendly defaults: salted user_id_hash and api_key_hash at rest, short default TTLs on user-scoped features, documented PII model — prompt content should not land in beava, but identifiers do. 11) Optional embedding-distance / cosine-similarity primitive, or a documented producer-side pattern for jailbreak-similarity scoring. 12) A streaming admin / debug surface ('top-k api_keys by guardrail_hit_rate last 5 min', 'top-k agents by tool_call rate') so SOC / safety analysts can drive incident response. 13) Audit / structured log of admin writes for SOC 2 and EU AI Act Article 12 — even if beava is not the audit store, its own admin plane needs to be auditable.
risk_and_non_goals.trigger_action_required: Yes — this domain genuinely needs an event-driven trigger primitive (e.g., 'when (api_key).tpm_1m crosses 200k, throttle', 'when (agent_id).identical_tool_calls_60s crosses 50, kill session', 'when (tenant).$_spend_hour crosses budget, page on-call', 'when (api_key).guardrail_hit_rate_5m crosses 10/min, quarantine key'). Inline-decision reads cover the synchronous path on the next request, but the asynchronous 'kill the runaway session / page the team / push a virtual-key block to the gateway' path is wasteful as polling. Competing AI gateways already implement this as webhooks (Portkey alerts, Truefoundry budget alerts, Helicone alerts) — a feature backend that exposes the trigger primitive natively would compress the stack.
